As a recreational runner, you might follow the plan almost to the letter, The threshold sessions go well, the easy runs stay easy. Over the weeks, progress arrives: slightly better pace at the same heart rate, a bit more spring in your step, a training log that looks exactly as it should.
And then it shifts. The small signals creep in, often tangled up with a hectic daily life. They usually start quietly: a staircase at home that suddenly feels heavier, even though everything else seems normal. A few days later, sleep changes, you wake a little earlier than usual without quite knowing why. Then come the mental adjustments: a session gets shuffled around, and you start bargaining with yourself in the name of discipline. Eventually, progress stalls.
What could have been a simple course correction over a few days turns into weeks of stagnation. And because the early signals went unheeded, it can take months to return to where you started.
Overtraining is feared by athletes—yet it lacks precise objective markers.
That's exactly why you must learn to recognize the subtle signals the body sends before it's too late, and why I recommend tracking a few objective measures alongside your feel.
In this chapter, you'll learn how to identify, avoid, and if necessary recover from overtraining, drawing on both scientific research and hard-won practical experience.
The Early Warnings Resting Heart Rate
Even as a recreational runner, I still track resting heart rate every night as a window into load, along with HRV, which we'll get to later. A rise in ear-y-morning heart rate is a classic sign that the body isn't firing on all cylinders.
Fortunately, you don't need fancy equipment to monitor this.
How to measure resting heart rate correctly
*   Measure immediately after waking, before getting up
*   Lie still, completely relaxed
*   Count heart rate for 30 seconds × 2, or use a heart rate monitor
*   Log the value in your training diary
*   Watch for trends over 7-14 days

Modern monitors are now reliable enough that nighttime readings work well as a baseline. Barron and colleagues showed as carly as 1985 that overtrained endurance athletes displayed impaired hormonal response in the HPA axis during insulin-induced hypoglycemia. In practice, this kind of axis disruption can show up over time as altered resting heart rate, alongside fatigue and performance decline.
Interpreting changes in morning heart rate
*   Normal variation: +2-3 beats from day to day
*   Concerning: +5 beats above baseline for 3+ days
*   Alarming: +8-10 beats sustained over a week
*   Critical: +10-15 beats that don't normalize with rest
But absolute numbers are not everything. A gradual climb from 45 to 48 to 51 over two weeks is just as telling as a sudden spike. In my experience, resting heart rate often serves as an early warning that load has grown too heavy, typically surfacing a few days before the body starts shutting down in other ways.
I am not a fan of letting numbers alone dictate training, but when these patterns persist over several days, they should not be ignored.
One point matters here especially: do not push hard and fast on the sessions that follow. Running a threshold workout with an emerging infection carries far less risk than an intensive effort up near 90-95% of maximum heart rate.
Sleep Symptoms
Sleep disturbances are often the first symptom of overtraining syndrome, long before performance falters. Endocrine hormones are essential for physiological responses and adaptations during exercise, and they shape the recovery phase by modulating anabolic and catabolic processes. When these hormones drift out of balance, sleep is usually the first to suffer.
WARNING SIGNALS IN SLEEP PATTERNS:
*   Difficulty falling asleep despite exhaustion
*   Waking between 03:00 and 05:00 (cortisol peak)
*   Restless sleep with frequent position changes
* 
*   Night sweats without obvious cause
*   Nightmares or unusually vivid dreams
*   Feeling wired even though you're spent
Research shows that chronically elevated cortisol from daily training disrupts the normal circadian rhythm. This sets off a vicious cycle: poor sleep leads to poorer recovery, which breeds more stress, which degrades sleep further still.
On the practical side, keep a simple sleep diary, rate quality from 1 to 10 each morning, note waking times and how you feel. Look for patterns that track with hard training, and consider HRV measurement at night or in the morning for objective data.
Loss of Motivation
Loss of motivation and training enjoyment isn't a weakness, but the body's defense mechanism. It is rarely wise to train hard when the body is already signaling "enough."

Overtraining is characterized by reduced sport-specific performance, accelerated fatiguability, and subjective symptoms of stress. Mental warning signals you must take seriously include anxiety before planned quality sessions, constant rumination over training volume, the sense that training has become obligation rather than joy, fading competitive drive, and heightened emotional volatility.
Performance Stagnation
Here lies one of the biggest traps. When results plateau, the first impulse is often to train harder. A common mistake is confusing overtraining
with underperformance.
Objective signs of stagnation show up when threshold pace feels progressively heavier. Getting heart rate and speed up during sessions becomes a struggle, as if you can't quite access the gears you normally have.
This relates primarily to muscular factors. The muscles' ability to mobilize diminishes, and every extra effort seems to cost far more than it should.
Recovery drags on longer than normal, and simple activities that call on the muscles a bit more (climbing stairs, for instance) feel unexpectedly heavy.

In response to a standardized high-intensity effort, overtrained athletes show lower heart rate, lactate, and plasma cortisol response. This paradox--the body's failure to mount a normal stress response-—is a hallmark of overtraining.
Key point: During any ten-day training stretch, at least one session should feel genuinely good, light legs, the temptation to pile on more work. If that feeling never arrives within that window, it's time to hit the brakes.
Heavy Thighs
One of the most telling signs of emerging overtraining is how the thighs feel during everyday movement. Climbing stairs suddenly becomes an ordeal, and even ordinary walking can feel strangely laborious.
This traces back to changes in muscle tone and elasticity that follow a predictable arc. In the early phase of overtraining, muscle tone climbs while elasticity remains relatively intact. You notice the heaviness especially on stairs, as if the thighs weigh twice what they should. This is the body's first signal that the muscles aren't recovering properly between sessions.
Push on without adequate rest, and the condition progresses. Muscle tone can then paradoxically collapse, while the muscles turn tight and inelastic.
This is serious overtraining. Now even small efforts feel nearly impossible. You may notice tingling in the thighs at night, minor cramps in stiff tissue, and a pervasive sense that the legs simply won't cooperate.
I describe this further in the stair test below. The key point is that this is an carly and reliable warning signal. Interestingly, short strides and 45/15 intervals can actually help you climb out of this state by stimulating the muscles in the right way. Combined with massage when needed, this can be the path back to normal tone and elasticity.
The Stair Test
A smart, practical way to catch overtraining and overload early is the stair test.
My experience as both athlete and clinician is that early overtraining is primarily a muscular phenomenon. Before resting heart rate budges, before sleep deteriorates, before motivation wavers, subtle changes occur in the muscles
that most people miss.

It comes down to two things: elevated muscle tone, the baseline tension in the muscle fibers, combined with reduced elasticity in the tissue itself. When muscles do not get enough time to normalize between sessions, they linger in a state ofheightened tension. Simultaneously, they lose their natural elasticity, the capacity to contract and stretch efficiently. This does not happen overnight, but builds gradually over days and weeks of inadequate recovery.
What is striking is how consistent this experience is among athletes who have encountered genuine overtraining.
Ask them about the first sign, and most will tell you the same thing: stairs suddenly got heavy.
Not running, not intervals, just the simple act of walking up an ordinary staircase felt different. Heavier. More demanding than it should be.
This hands us a valuable tool for early detection. Instead of waiting until
you are deep in overtraining, you can use this as a warning system.
Daily execution of the stair test:
*   Choose a short flight of stairs you can climb daily, same stairs, same number of steps, ideally at the same time of day
*   Climb with conscious attention to how the thigh muscles feel on the way up and when you reach the top; focus specifically on the muscular sensation
*   Over time, you'll develop sensitivity to your normal variations
*   Days when the stairs feel unusually heavy, when the thighs seem stiff or sluggish, may be an early signal that recovery isn't keeping pace with load

Ideally, you'd learn to feel the thigh muscles directly, assessing tone and elasticity by touch. The stair test gives you access to much of the same information in a simple, reproducible way anyone can learn.
Used systematically over several weeks, the stair test will paint a surprisingly precise picture of muscular condition and recovery. Try it, and you'll be impressed by how much information your body offers when you learn to listen.
Muscular State
The stair test captures something important: the muscles respond before much else does, often before resting heart rate rises, before sleep deteriorates, before motivation fades. The muscles know first.
I keep returning to this point: muscular factors are the true ceiling on training, especially in running. Yes, you can overtrain through sheer accumulated load. But what governs how you feel week to week, your receptivity to training, the good days and the bad, comes down mostly to the balance you strike in the muscular system.
This matters most when load creeps toward the edge of what your body can handle. But as both runner and general practitioner, I am struck by how important it remains even for runners training just three or four times a week.
I can slide straight into muscular overtraining (elevated tone, depleted elasticity) on just four to six sessions a week if I push the threshold work a touch too hard. And this despite more than twenty-five years of systematic training, ten of them at two or three sessions a day.
Muscles are perishable, and they demand continuous attention and adjust-ment. It takes surprisingly little to upset the balance: a few weeks where intensity runs slightly too high or recovery windows fall slightly too short.
Peak form, daily form, training receptivity, overtraining: muscular state sits at the center of all of it.
Muscular state is the bounce you feel in your stride on the really good days.
It is the weight in every footfall when things turn sluggish. It is the surprise when race day suddenly feels far better than the tune-up a few days earlier.
Learn to read your muscular state, and you gain an entirely new dimension in your training.
You can also assess the muscles directly. Wrap a broad grip around the muscle belly. Notice how tense it is, how much mass fills your hand. Shift the muscle sideways and feel how freely it moves; high tone limits displacement.
Then release. The speed at which it springs back is the elasticity.

Why Threshold Training Provides Control
Higher intensity doesn't just raise muscle tone more, it also prolongs the time needed to return to normal. You lose control of the recovery window. With a threshold-based model, you keep this under far better control. Threshold sessions, even doubles, leave roughly the same muscular imprint each time.
That predictability is the payoff: low risk, high reward.
Want to Go Deeper?
In Chapter 15 you'll find precise definitions, a muscular reference point drawn from thousands of palpations, the story of my master's thesis with Professor Per Brodal, and guidance on actively optimizing muscle tone through the training cycle and into competition. The material is detailed, but it's there for those who want to dig in.
Objective Markers
HRV Measurement
Heart Rate Variability is often presented as the gold standard for training monitoring but reality is more nuanced than the marketing suggests. The most common response to overload is a progressive drop in HRV. Yet several studies have reported rising HRV trends in overtrained endurance athletes.
This paradox can likely be explained by two autonomic presentations of overtraining:
TWO PRESENTATIONS OF OVERTRAINING
*   Sympathetic-dominant presentation: disturbed sleep, irritability, "wired but tired," sometimes elevated resting HR and reduced HRV.
*   Parasympathetic-hyperactivity presentation (often in endurance athletes): unusually low or hard-to-raise HR, reduced max HR, profound fatigue, low drive, depressive symptoms; HRV may be relatively high in some cases but is variable.
218
The research is mixed. An older study from 2003 (Bosquet) concluded that HRV during sleep doesn't appear to be a valid marker for overtraining in male endurance athletes. Other work (Mourot et al., 2004) hints at the opposite, but findings are method-dependent, underscoring the complexity.

Using HRV effectively requires measuring consistently: same time, same position, same conditions. Track seven-day rolling averages and stay alert to both increases and decreases. Always pair HRV with subjective markers, and resist overreacting to single readings.
Practical tip: Personally, I find HRV most useful for catching illness before it fully arrives. HRV is surprisingly sensitive to brewing infection. When I spot a rapid, unexplained overnight shift, I tread carefully with the next hard session. Patients report the same-many now track HRV and notice the dip just before symptoms hit.
Recent research (Alfonso et al., 2025) emphasizes that daily HRV should be read alongside resting heart rate and perceived well-being. Low HRV combined with elevated resting heart rate and poor sleep points to compromised recovery, even if heart rate during the session looks normal. Add in perceived feel and perhaps warm-up heart rate, and you have a solid read on how receptive the body is to training that day.

For those with access to lactate testing, shifts in lactate profile offer invaluable insight into overtraining.

Performance Tests Every Fourth Week
Systematic testing is essential for catching overtraining early. A detailed training diary helps prevent it, and guides your return if you've already slipped into overtraining syndrome.
For lactate-based training, the recommended approach is a submaximal standard test every four weeks. Begin with 10 minutes of warm-up, then run 3-5 x 5 minutes at fixed paces. Compare against previous tests by correlating lactate with heart rate and pace; look for patterns.
As covered earlier, in a good phase you want low lactate, high heart rate, and high pace. If your training is built on field tests or VDOT rather than lactate, periodic retesting gives you almost equally useful data.
Blood Work
As a physician, 1 routinely order blood work when athletes present with overtraining symptoms. But labs must be read in context, never in isolation. For mapping overtraining, muscular state matters far more than any single value.
The first priority is ruling out deficiency or systemic illness masquerading as overtraining. A practical panel includes ferritin, vitamin B12, vitamin D, TSH and free T4, a basic metabolic panel, liver enzymes, and a complete blood count (including hemoglobin and platelets). Testosterone, cortisol, and creatine kinase (CK) can also be useful.
For CK, there is no single "right" cutoff. Baselines vary widely, hard training can elevate CK for 1 to 3 days (sometimes into the thousands), and the most useful signal is the trend over time together with symptoms and recovery.

My own CK ranged from roughly 100 to 2,000 U/L during hard blocks. The point stands: don't fixate on one number. Look at the trajectory and the full clinical picture.
Adjustment Strategies
Reduce Intensity, Not Volume
When overtraining looms, the instinct is often to slash volume drastically.
Research—and my own experience—suggest this is often the wrong move.
When overtraining is suspected, keep heart rate around 70% of max on most sessions and give the body time to rebuild a solid base without excess stress. Cut volume by perhaps 20-30%, but combine this with regular 30/30 or 45/15 sessions; maintaining muscular stimuli is critical. Otherwise, you risk a rocky return to normal training.
Easy running promotes blood flow, preserves mitochondrial function, lowers cortisol, and maintains training habits and mental health, all of which work in your favor when climbing out of an overtrained state. When you add 30/30 or 45/15 work (and possibly light hill strides), you stimulate the muscles across the full loading spectrum.
In muscular terms, you recruit a wider range of motor units, restore a better feel for the tissue, and, in my experience, improve your chances of recovering from an overtrained state.
Sample training week for working out of early overtraining signs:
*   2 complete rest days per week, ideally consecutive
*   1 session of 45/15 × 10-15, with each rep progressively faster to span the muscular range
*   1 session of 30/30, similarly structured
*   I session of 15-20 x hill strides, progressively faster, roughly 60 m each, aim to reactivate the muscles
*   2 sessions of easy running, 20-30 minutes
*   Combine with massage and hot baths when possible
Buffer Weeks
In line with the principle that short intervals can reset overloaded muscles, consider building in a super-easy week with a short-interval focus roughly every fourth week once you're functioning again. Think of it as a butter against sliding back into overtraining.
Structure for super-easy week (every 4th week):
*   Volume: 60-70% of normal
*   Intensity: At most one threshold-pace session
*   Quality emphasis: Shorter intervals like 45/15
*   Easy sessions: Very easy, though volume can rise on a longer weekend run
*   Include massage and hot/cold baths to amplify the muscular reset
I also recommend using concrete methods to gauge the body's state during sessions, combined with that day's resting heart rate. It needn't be complicated.
I've long relied on a traffic light model that I developed during my competitive years and used systematically to adjust my training. As a recreational runner, I still use a simplified version.
The Traffic Light Model

The traffic light model offers a different way of thinking about load. You adjust each day's session dynamically, based on objective markers gathered during the workout itself. Supplement with resting heart rate from that morning.
The result: you add volume on the days when the body is maximally recep-tive, and you back off on days when it clearly isn't. You extract maximum benefit from responsive training days while steering clear of overtraining when the body is most vulnerable.
I used this principle actively throughout my career, and I encourage you to develop your own version.
My traffic light model looked like this:
Green light: Low warm-up heart rate and high heart rate at the threshold (confirmed by lactate). If resting heart rate and muscular feel aligned, it was a perfect day for hard work. On these days, I extended the session on the fly, up to 30-40% beyond what was planned.
Yellow light: Normal values = complete as planned.
Red light: High warm-up heart rate or low threshold heart rate combined with
elevated lactate early in the session = abort the workout or stop after warm-up.
Then one day off, one day easy, before resuming normal load.

Four days before my 13:06 for 5000 meters, 1 recorded a threshold heart rate of 181, just 11 beats below max, at 3.0 mmol/L lactate and 2:52 per kilometer pace (4:37 per mile). Resting heart rate was low, and the thighs felt lively on stairs: optimal form and a clear green light for hard training.

A simpler version for you might look like this:
Green light: Low resting heart rate, possibly high HRV, light feeling on stairs that day, heart rate rising quickly to target pace, relatively high speed. Inese are reliable markers of a green day.
Yellow light: The same parameters sitting in average territory.

Red light: Any of the green-light factors sharply off, very high resting heart rate, very low HRV, or unusually heavy legs on stairs, is enough to pull back.
If the warm-up feeling and the first rep's numbers are also poor, it's a rest day.
You can also run a fixed threshold rep of 3-6 minutes before every interval session, following a standard warm-up. Done consistently, this yields valuable data. The goal is to build a flexible framework grounded in how the body is actually functioning that day (felt and measured then act on what you find.
Conclusion
Overtraining is not a sign of weakness, but ambition that outran control.
The tools in this chapter are simple: a staircase, a resting heart rate, a grip around the muscle belly, a traffic light system that forces you to ask the right question before every hard session. None of it is complicated. The hard part is acting on what you find.
The runners who last are not the ones who train the hardest, but the ones who learn when to stop, and who trust that stopping today is what lets them train again tomorrow.
If the practical parts of this book are enough for you, you now have what you need. But if you want to understand the deeper mechanics behind what you have been applying —why threshold training works the way it does, how the model actually came together, and where the final percentages hide—read on.

Summary
*   THE EARLY SIGNALS. Stair that suddenly feel heavy. Sleep that breaks between 3 and 5 AM. Loss of motivation. A threshold pace that feels progressively harder. These arrive before anything dramatic—and they're the ones to act on.
*   THE STAIR TEST. Climb the same stairs daily and notice how the thighs feel. Over time you develop a baseline. Days when they feel stiff or sluggish are an early signal that recovery isn't keeping pace with load.
*   RESTING HEART RATE. A rise of 5 beats above baseline for three or more days is concerning. A sustained rise of 8-10 beats over a week is alarming. Track trends over 7-14 days, not single readings.
*   THE MUSCLES KNOW FIRST. Before heart rate budges, before sleep deteriorates, before motivation fades. It takes surprisingly little to upset the balance.

T
he Norwegian Method was not designed as a finished system. It grew through curiosity, trial and error, and one simple control principle: intensity must be precise enough to be tolerated week after week.
The preceding parts have given you the model: the principles, the structure, the sessions. That is enough to train by. But some readers will want more. This part is for coaches who need to know why, not just how. For runners who want precise tools. And for the simply curious who want the full picture.
Understanding why requires knowing where it came from. The story of how the model was structured explains why it looks the way it does. From a chance exchange year in Illinois to double threshold experiments in South Africa, through Kenya, through Peter Coe in London, through Per Halle's training diary from 1972. It was not a straight line. It was trial, error, measurement, adjustment, and gradually a structure that made sense.
From origins, we move to application. Lactate measurement in practice is more than taking a sample. It is learning to read a curve: what a flat profile tells you, what drift means, when to adjust pace and when to end the session. The decision rules are concrete and operational. If you do not use a lactate meter, the principles still apply; skim the technical sections and focus on the summaries.
The technical details raise a deeper question: why does double threshold work at all? The physiological rationale addresses multiple limiting factors simultaneously, the general stress response, the muscular load, and the timing between stimulus and recovery.
That leads to what may be the most overlooked topic in distance running.
Muscle tone gets its own deeper chapter because it deserves one. This is where most people fly blind —and where the final percentages live.
Finally, a look forward at which technologies may change how we train, and which questions remain open.
Some of this is technical, but I have written it as practically as I can. The method came into being through practical experimentation, and that is how
it is best explained.
We start with the history.

In the spring of 1996, I found myself standing on a track in Elmhurst, Illinois, in one of the more absurd coaching situations in high school running history.
On one side stood Peter Coe, father and lifelong coach of Sebastian Coe, who had flown in from London to help motivate and inspire a group of American high school runners. On the other side stood Joe Newton, who earlier that day had relayed Arthur Lydiard's instructions from New Zealand to the same group. Even Coe seemed amused that Newton had managed to rope in both sides of distance running royalty for a high school team.
Two giants of distance running, one the godfather of modern endurance training and the broad aerobic base, the other the architect of multi-tier training and much of modern middle-distance running. And in the middle: me, a seventeen-year-old exchange student from Norway who had ended up there because he wrote "I like to run" on an application form.
I did not understand, at the time, how unlikely that scene was, but I do now.
And I did not understand that I was absorbing two fundamentally different training philosophies at the same time, one built on volume and patience, the other on precision. The tension between those two ideas would stay with me for years.
In many ways, resolving it is what influenced the Norwegian Method-taking Lydiard's patience and Coe's demand for precision, but redirecting that precision toward intensity control.
That is how training systems actually develop, not through a single insight, but through the gradual collision of influences, experiments, and questions that refuse to go away. This chapter traces that process from its earliest moments through nearly three decades.

It did not start as a system, but with a problem:
How can a runner without extreme innate abilities train more and better without breaking down?
That question drove everything that followed. Training methods tend to be presented as finished packages, as if someone sat down one day and constructed them from scratch. That is not how it works. What is described in this book grew in waves of trial, error, measurement, and adjustment. Each influence added something. Each failure removed something. The result is thousands of lactate measurements, countless failed experiments, and a long series of corrections that only made sense in hindsight.
Along the way, many have contributed: coaches, physiologists, runners, through conversations, ideas, and questions that shaped how I think and helped me structure the framework. Some ideas came from coaches I met by chance.
Others from physiologists who asked questions I had not considered. Most came from my own body, which showed me again and again what worked and what did not.
The method is not finished. It will continue to evolve, and you should be part of that process. Ask questions and experiment, but don't blindly copy what worked for someone else. Do it in a controlled way, one variable at a time, with measurements that give you answers.
That is how this method came to be, and how it will get better.
1995-1996: York High School and Joe Newton
In 1995, I was a high school student in Norway with an exchange application and not much to fill in. Most fields stayed empty. Under my interests, I wrote the only thing I knew to be true: I like to run.
That single line landed me at York High School in Elmhurst, Illinois, a school that would turn out to be one of the strongest running environments in American high school history. Someone, somewhere, had heard they had a good program, so there I went.
Joe Newton was already a legend. He had built York into a national institution in cross-country, with a record few have come close to in American high school running. The movie The Long Green Line would later tell that story. As mentioned, Newton was a disciple of Arthur Lydiard—not just inspired by

him, but in direct contact through shared clinics and phone calls. In 1988, he became the first high school track coach brought onto the US Olympic staff.
I arrived from Norway with a completely different frame of reference. With Newton, the volume was high, but it was never just mileage. Intervals were woven into the system as a fixed rhythm through the week. Every Wednesday:
25x400 meters. I learned that session there, and it later became one of the central quality sessions in the Norwegian Method.
That year became a personal turning point. By spring, I had run the fastest high school two-mile time in the US that year. For me, it was proof of what can happen when you land in an environment where load is not just executed but managed, repeated, and tolerated.
It was through Newton that 1 was introduced to Peter Coe, and with that introduction came my first experience with double threshold.
Takeaway: Volume and intervals simultaneously. Not either-or. Both, every week.
1995-1996: Peter Coe and the First
Double Threshold Sessions
Before the 1984 Olympics, Newton had worked with Sebastian Coe. Through that connection, I met Sebastian's father and coach.
Peter Coe gave me my first taste of double threshold: two controlled sessions on the same day, a way to accumulate more threshold work without any single session becoming too large. I was focused on 800 and 1500 meters at the time, but the logic was immediately clear. It stayed with me.
Peter trained by a structured approach with several distinct intensity levels.
To compensate for phases with lower mileage, he used what he called top-up mileage weeks, periods where conditioning load was compressed into fewer days. In the bitter Chicago wind, I ran my first double threshold on the Prairie Path in the winter of 1995-96.
We stayed in contact until 2002 through emails, his visits to Norway, and stays with him in Chelsea, and ran some of Sebastian's old training routes.
One was an overgrown hill by the Thames that became my first experience with systematic hill training. Peter used two formats: long efforts of 600-800 meters and shorter, steeper sprints of 180-200 meters.
The short hill workout is now a standard element in a typical winter week of the Norwegian Method.

Takeaway: Compressing threshold work into two sessions on the same day yields more volume at lower muscular cost per session. Hill sessions provide benefits beyond intensity alone.
1997: Indiana University and Sam Bell
After a year back in Norway, I started at Indiana University in the fall of 1997.
There I trained under Sam Bell, who coached Bob Kennedy, the first non-Af-rican to break 13:00 for 5000 meters.
Kennedy had just finished a rest period after a demanding international season. I was in the middle of cross-country with form that was rising fast, which meant I could keep up with his interval work. At the time, Kennedy trained alongside a group of Kenyans that included Daniel Komen, the world record holder for 3000 meters. Those conversations sparked an interest in Kenyan training that I would later pursue firsthand.
One point from Kennedy stuck with me. He explained that Kenyans have a more finely calibrated sense of perceived exertion than most non-African runners they hit the right intensity more intuitively. He was right, and I later confirmed it through lactate measurements at Kenyan training camps.
I left Indiana after just one year. The training model did not suit my physi-ology, but seeing the world's fastest non-African runner up close gave valuable insight into what a top performance environment looks like. I also continued developing double threshold, stacking extra sessions close together-often in the evenings.
Takeaway: Intuition can be extremely precise, but it must be translated into a system if it is to be replicable.
1998-1999: Back to Norway and Per Halle
Late in 1998, I returned to Norway close to quitting running. My former coach Per Halle welcomed me back. Per had run 13:27 and finished seventh in the Olympic final in Munich 1972, the same race where Lasse Virén won and Steve Prefontaine finished fourth. He lived a few hundred meters from my childhood home and had followed me since I was young. Another of many strange coincidences in my running career— one I didn't appreciate until later.
We talked at length about my training problems. I already had many pieces I understood were valuable, but could not quite put everything together. Finally, we made an unusual decision: would copy his training diary from 1972 for the 1999 season. Session by session.

From January 1999, I increased the volume to 180 km (112 miles) per week to mirror him. We agreed to consciously lower the intensity to ensure an aerobic focus. All training was done with a significant buffer. Later measurements confirmed I had been hitting the Golden Zone. I also integrated the double threshold elements I already had with me. Many of Per's typical winter sessions, such as 6-minute and 10-minute intervals, later became central to the typical Norwegian Method winter week.
The experiment ended with 13:22 for 5000 meters, built on awareness of intensity and a consistently conservative strategy. It sounds simple, but this was a turning point—proof that more aerobic load under control strengthened everything else. I was fortunate to hit this load primarily using heart rate, but I also learned that "more" had to be controlled otherwise a limit would come sooner than necessary.
Further into 1999, I engaged in even more extreme experimentation: up to three or four sessions daily, threshold sessions with a combined volume of 26 km (16 miles), daily threshold training inspired by Coe's top-up mileage weeks.
The experimentation never stopped—but the lesson held.
Takeaway: "More" only works if "more" is controlled. Uncontrolled more breaks you down before it builds you.
1999-2002: The Lactate Project
The next step came through a project run by the Norwegian Athletics Federation and the Norwegian Olympic Sports Centre. Espen Tønnessen, Orjan Madsen, and Frank Evertsen were part of it.
Frank brought practical experience with field measurement of lactate and years of work with Kenyan runners. As part of the project, lactate was measured during three weekend training camps, not yet as a steering tool, but to check actual load against intention. By 2000, I was using it on every quality session. It gave far more precise session control and evaluation, and enabled a dynamic training model that could be continually adjusted around the fixed principles I was aiming for.
From 2000 to 2002, Frank and I worked together. The lactate data added a new layer of precision to the structural framework and intensity principles I had built through the preceding years. Frank also introduced me to altitude training, which led to my first trip to Kenya in 2000. Altitude training and the Norwegian Method go hand in hand. It acts as a catalyst for the principles the method already stands for.
Takeaway: Lactate measurement became a tool for making load repeatable and enabling work closer to the edge.
Kenya: The Pattern That Emerged
Kenya became a reality check. I spent months in partly remote areas training with some of the best runners in the world. I saw enormous talent and depth.
More importantly, I saw that many of the best hit the right load intuitively.
The lactate meter made it possible to actually see this, not guess.
Equally important: on hard sessions above threshold, the same runners did not push lactate as high as Norwegians typically did. They held back there too, with a flat, controlled curve.
Kenya did not give me the recipe, but confirmation that I was on the right track and more data to work with.
Takeaway: The best do not always push the hardest. They hit the right load more often. It is reproducible, but it should be measured.
2002-2003: The Transition to a Structured Model
After a difficult 2002 season, the collaboration with Evertsen ended and I trained alone again. The principles still worked, but I needed to fine-tune them further to get back to where I had been. Recovery had become harder, and the margins were smaller than before. I ran 13:35 at best, a long way from my 13:09 personal best at the time.
In hindsight, that period was essential. The smaller margins forced adjustments that made the model more precise than it had ever been. When there is less room for error, every variable has to earn its place.
Several adjustments emerged from this period. I removed the intensive
1000-meter intervals at 5-8 mmol/L entirely from winter training. I reduced the volume of single threshold sessions but doubled up with systematic double threshold sessions several times per week, and I shifted from two hard weeks followed by one easier week to structurally flat weeks.
The shift to flatter weeks came after a conversation with Paula Radcliffes coach Alex Stanton. My manager Ståle Jan Frøynes used all his contacts to arrange it. I sat in my student apartment in Oslo, dialed his number, and had a long conversation where he dissected their experlence before we looked at how it could solve my challenges. Combined with increased Focus on double threshold, it allowed steady progress without the same risk of overload.
Takeaway: The crucial thing was not only the isolated "two threshold sessions on the same day." It was also the weekly structure that made it possible.

2003-2004: Alnes, Frøynes, and the Final Structure During this period, I began working with Leif Olav Alnes-sprint coach for Geir Moen, and later for Karsten Warholm, who in 2021 shattered the 400-meter hurdles world record. Alnes had helped me with sprint and explosive training since 2000-2001 and had influenced my thinking about consolidating hard sessions.
Before the 2003 season, I asked him to join my training sessions. It took a long time to convince him, but he finally agreed after I had laid out exactly what I needed help with. He is one of the sharpest training minds I have encountered.
I pitched structural ideas, and Alnes used his understanding of how to balance concentrated load with recovery to shape the training weeks. His experience with sprinters helped me cut total threshold load per session and instead focus on double threshold with somewhat shorter sessions. He stood calmly beside me, checked lactate, and challenged my thinking over a two-year period.
In the winter of 2004, everything clicked into place. When I look back at my training diary from that time, it was the first time I followed what was later recognized as the typical Norwegian Method week—in the base period:

That summer, I set my personal best with 13:06.39 in Rome, the fastest 5000-meter time in Europe that year by a five-second margin, in what I think was a suboptimal race. For comparison, 19 athletes ran faster than this in Europe in 2024. Shoes play a role, but training does too.

2004-2006: Transfer to Other Runners
From 2004 to 2006, I trained alongside steeplechaser Bjørnar Kristensen, who was coached by Eric Toogood. He was one of very few athletes I actually trained with. The method was controversial, and few wanted to commit to it fully at the time. We modified his training to the same model, double threshold sessions, lower intensity on easy days, systematic altitude training. Kristensen ran 8:16
for 3000-meter steeplechase.
Toogood also coached another young athlete: Henrik Ingebrigtsen, brother of Jakob. He took the training model and the exact sessions to Henrik, whom he guided until just a few months before Henrik's first European Championship gold in 2012. Henrik finished fifth at the Olympics that same summer, only 21 years old. The X-session element he introduced was Coe-style short hill sprints instead of flat ground.
Takeaway: Once the framework is robust, it can transfer between athletes with surprisingly few changes, and the smartest tweaks tend to be small.
2009-2013: The Bridge to the Ingebrigtsen Era
From 2009—and intensified between 2011 and 2013—I had direct contact with Gert Ingebrigtsen: phone calls, emails, text messages, concrete advice on session-to-session planning.

One of the first things I recommended was systematizing double threshold sessions on the same day, also for a 1500-meter runner. Focus on intervals rather than continuous hard sessions. Strengthening altitude training as base work, tapering, and competition preparation. And repeated emphasis that development of the anaerobic threshold must be the core focus over time.
We had long conversations about intensity control with a lactate meter, especially at the threshold, and which intensity levels versus total kilometer load to aim for in both summer and winter.
In 2022, I was contacted by the family of my former coach Per Halle to help his grandson, Simen Halle Haugen, a 13:37 runner for 5000 meters. I worked with him over a full annual cycle.
During this period, he was integrated into the Ingebrigtsen training group during their altitude camps in Sierra Nevada. They followed pretty much as a carbon copy—the same weekly structure, lactate value and sessions that had been developed eighteen years earlier. Even the training days were the same:
Tuesday's 2000-meter intervals in the morning, 400s in the evening; Thursday's
10-minute intervals in the morning, 1000s in the evening; the X-Factor element on Saturday. 180 km (112 miles) per week. Lactate sitting right between 2-3 mmol/L. A clear example of successful knowledge transfer.
Takeaway: When intensity is tightly controlled and the week is built around repeatable anchors, a model can scale from one runner to an entire group, and still look almost identical decades later.
2019-Today: From Norwegian Niche to Global Reach Norway has 5.5 million inhabitants, about the same as Minnesota. Yet the level Norwegian athletes achieve in middle distance, long distance, and triathlon is world class. The model is now used across all the strong Norwegian training environments.
Double threshold eventually became a term that took on a life of its own.
At the same time, strong international environments began adopting the weekly structure correctly: controlled threshold volume, flat weeks, minimal stress on easy days, focus on control rather than variation for variation's sake.
Mike Smith at Northern Arizona University was one of the first in the
USA. NAU became the first major American college program to systematically implement double threshold and has since become a dominant force with multiple NCAA titles.

In Europe, Swedish runners like Kalle Berglund and Andreas Almgren adopted the Ingebrigtsen training directly. Algren trains at an even higher volume than Jakob, often over 200 km (124 miles) per week, with double threshold on Tuesdays and Thursdays. The results: Swedish records at 1500 m, 5000 m, 10,000 m, and half marathon, plus the European record at 5000 meters in 2025.
George Mills describes his week structure like this: Monday, Wednesday, and Friday are two easy runs, morning and evening; Tuesday and Thursday are double threshold; Saturday is a harder session with jogging afterward; Sunday is a long run. In June 2025, he set the British record for 5000 meters, nearly seven seconds faster than Mo Farah's record, which had stood for fourteen years.
In correspondence with me, former Norwegian national triathlon-team coach Arild Tveiten described the model used by Norwegian triathletes including Kristian Blummenfelt—a framework that had by then spread from distance running into endurance sport more broadly—as built on high volume at low intensity, threshold values typically around 2.5 to 3.0 mmol/L, and regular double-threshold structure. These were the same principles I had published more than a decade earlier: "When estimating the threshold according to these protocols, we typically find that the anaerobic threshold lands around 2.5-3.0 mmol/L lactate rather than the typical 4 mmol/L ... We do a lot of double-threshold."
He also described a standardized 4-day altitude cycle: "Day 1: two threshold sessions/double threshold running, one easy session. Day 2: long easy (5-8 hours workout). Day 3: two threshold sessions, one easy. Day 4: very easy training of about 2 hours easy training of choice."
This is the same narrow, repeatable threshold band I define in this book as the Golden Zone, embedded within the same broader logic of double threshold supported by large volumes of easy work.
Takeaway: The model works across distances and endurance sports because the physiology is the same. Only the application changes.

Technology makes it easier to copy. Lactate measurement has become far more accessible-helpful, but it also means some runners have become more number-driven than necessary. Shoes and surfaces have changed the tolerance threshold. Modern footwear reduces much of the acute load and can make higher volumes of quality work possible. But they do not remove the funda mental law: muscle tone must still drop between training loads.
The model's dynamic elements are being stretched. Jakob Ingebrigtsen and the world's best middle-distance runners have integrated significantly more intensive elements during summer. That is natural and distance-specific. It took me ten years to arrive at the weekly structure they use in winter, and I simply did not have time to try more. Andreas Almgren provides a similar example: far higher volume on the track at high speed, such as 10 × 1000 m in the low 2:30s, corresponding to his 5000-meter pace. I suspect his lactate corresponds to what I experienced on my 1000-meter sessions before the change I made in 2003—"skipping over" the 3-5 mmol/L zone and concentrating on lactate from 5-7 (8) mmol/L. As described earlier, this is an area with significant gain weighed against risk.
Triathletes have expanded the framework further. Athletes like Blummen-felt use science to measure adaptation and load more precisely than lactate alone, integrating nutrition absorption and temperature under the expert guidance of coach Olav Alexander Bu.
Terms have become detached from the whole. "Double threshold" has for some become synonymous with "two threshold sessions." In the original sense, it means two threshold sessions placed within a much larger system. Done with an already too heavily loaded muscular system, the effect is questionable.
What you see across all of this is further individualization and distance-spe-cific adaptation. I welcome that. It supports the very point of the model: a fixed center, understanding of its importance, ability to measure precisely- then moving outward with curiosity to individualize and adapt, in parallel with careful control.
Through all of this, the core remains the same as it was in 1999: develop the anaerobic threshold as high as possible. Do it by training in a controlled way in the Golden Zone. Compress training into double sessions to get more volume near the threshold. Be careful with more intensive training, and always with measurement. Balance the muscular system. Test, adjust, test again. It is not more complicated than that.

But doing it well requires a control system that most people never learn, because they copy the structure without understanding how intensity is actu ally guided. They get the sessions right and the control wrong. That is where the method breaks down, not in the design, but in the execution, week after
week, session after session.
Ar an elite level, and for any serious runner pushing close to their ceiling, you can get through a hard session. The body adapts to single bouts of stress remarkably well.
What it cannot absorb is forty weeks at slightly wrong intensity-not dramatically wrong, just a fraction above where the training stimulus tips from productive to erosive. That margin is too small to feel in the moment. A 0.3 mmol/L drift in your threshold lactate readings across six weeks of training looks like nothing on any given Tuesday. Across a full season with serious load, it is the difference between arriving at your target race sharp and arriving depleted.
This is where lactate testing earns its place, not as a lab curiosity, but as the only tool that gives you session-level feedback precise enough to catch that drift before it compounds. Heart rate tells you how hard the cardiovascular system is working. Perceived effort tells you how the session feels. Lactate tells you what is actually happening in the muscle-whether the intensity is sitting where you intended it, or whether it has crept into a zone that looks identical from the outside but produces a fundamentally different training effect.
Elite runners and ambitious amateurs who have used lactate-guided training for years often describe the same thing: the numbers reveal sessions they would have sworn were easy as slightly too hard, and sessions they pushed through as surprisingly well-absorbed. That gap between perception and physiology is where most training errors live.
The next chapter is about closing that gap: how to read lactate curves, recognize drift, separate signal from noise, and make adjustments before the cost
shows up two weeks later.

Strip away all the mythology surrounding the Norwegian Method, and what remains at its core is precise intensity control over long periods of time-control that permits high training volume at the right, specific load. Not precision in the sense of "correct pace today," but precision in the sense that week after week you hit an internal load the body can tolerate, one that shifts capacity upward without the muscles gradually becoming the limiting factor.
This is also where most mistakes occur when people try to copy the method, especially double threshold training. They copy the structure but not the control system that made the structure possible. You can always push through a hard session. You cannot push through 40 weeks at slightly wrong intensity without paying the price—whether through stagnation, overload, or injury.
With high precision, the method yields high reward at low risk.
With low precision, high risk and low reward.
This chapter addresses how you actually control intensity at a technical level-not merely by finding the threshold, but by understanding curves, slopes, drift, error sources, and deviation patterns. The goal is for you to make decisions in real time during sessions and adjust correctly before you lose the rhythm of the week. This chapter is intentionally technical.
Breakpoint versus Zone
Before going further, a fundamental distinction that shapes everything that follows: the firen, a twen a true breakpoint and a zone.

Lactate is an indirect measure influenced by factors such as heat, glycogen availability, and measurement uncertainty. We cannot really speak of one certain breakpoint, even though the term is widely used and this book repeatedly refers to it as a "threshold." That is a simplification I am fully aware of.
Because intensity in the Golden Zone is set more conservatively than in many other training philosophies, it helps avoid real accumulation of load and fatigue from sitting right above the anaerobic threshold. This is one reason the method transfers so well for people switching from other approaches, even those claiming to be threshold-based.
The risk of setting one fixed intensity—for example, half marathon pace that sits right at the threshold—is that you will likely spend portions of the session above the load you should be at, due to the factors mentioned above.
You walk straight into overload risk, little by little, week after week.
Read the Golden Zone, then, for what it actually is: a zone. Conservative.
Safe. Effective. The safety margin is deliberately chosen, precisely because the inherent error margins demand it, to ensure you do not become too aggressive in your sessions. I mention this at the outset because I am fully aware of the debate around zones versus breakpoints. To put that discussion to rest:
I believe there is a training zone that is far more beneficial than others, both in terms of effect and load. And in my experience, it is both relatively specific and relatively narrow.
The Adaptation Period
Understanding that we are working with a zone rather than a fixed point leads naturally to a practical question: where should you start if you are new to this kind of training?
In earlier articles on my website, I described my experience of setting threshold session intensity below 3.0 mmol/L from the very beginning if you are not already well-versed in threshold training. I call it a normalization period, or adaptation period.
I still stand by this. Suppose your true threshold, measured in a lab, is 4.0 mmol/l, and you have little experience with threshold training. I strongly recommend setting your threshold sessions consistently in the typical Golden Zone of 2.3-3.0 mmol/L for four to six months before retesting.

For most people, this works surprisingly well for adapting the body to this new type of load. I suspect muscular factors play a role. With poor muscle condition-which most people have—and inadequate training load over time, the threshold tests at 4.0 mmol/L.
What I observe, though, is that even when 4.0 mmol/L is correctly measured at that moment, staying there often doesn't work-despite it being the measured value and despite continued threshold training.
In a sense, by continuing to train at that level, you carry with you whatever caused the threshold to sit at 4.0 mmol/L in the first place.
This small detail can actually cause athletes to abandon the model before they have really gotten started. Ir is a purcly practical adjustment, withour being able to fully explain it physiologically, and unsurprisingly, something no scientific studies have addressed.
Basic Session Management
Once you have established your working zone, the next step is learning how
to manage individual sessions within it.
Before a session, you should have a sense of the acceptable training zone once pace has stabilized. I often speak of 2.3-3.0 mmol/Llactate for many well-trained athletes, but this can easily extend to 2.1-3.3 mmol/L, as long as you are well recovered beforehand, and as long as you treat the ceiling and floor as signals to adjust, not targets to push against.

I recommend starting the session with a short warm-up followed by a single threshold effort of five minutes. This effort both warms up the system and provides vital information about how the session will go. Here is what it
typically tells you:
If heart rate rises quickly, pace is high, and lactate is low, that is the most reliable indicator that the body is primed for the session ahead. If heart rate is somewhat lower at the start but rises toward the end of the effort, pace is high or normal, and lactate is normal, this indicates high receptivity but with some muscular fatigue. It is precisely the muscular sluggishness that causes the heart rate response to lag, in my experience. Not a red flag, but worth noting.
In both cases, the session can proceed normally, and you can even add extra volume toward the end if the curve permits it. With the second scenario, you will more often see the curve rising toward the end of the session. If so, consider scheduling an extra easy day the following week, as this type of profile suggests emerging fatigue.
The Lactate Curve: What You Are Actually Reading The warm-up effort gives you a first indication of what to expect, but the real information emerges as the session unfolds. When you profile or measure during a session, you are essentially reading four things.
Baseline and early response
Some athletes get slightly higher early lactate than expected if the warm-up is too short, if they start too aggressively, or if they enter the session already revved up stress, caffeine, poor sleep. The warm-up effort described above addresses this and gives a useful picture of your current state.
I therefore recommend one to two threshold efforts of five minutes before sessions, as both a control mechanism and adaptation before the main work.
There is also a delayed lactate response, given its nature as an indirect measure, and this ensures a gradual buildup.
The curve's breakpoint and slope
A more distinct lactate breakpoint or accumulation signal can be useful, but the slope is more important. When the slope becomes steeper, you are in a range where a small pace increase requires disproportionately greater anaerobic support. This is precisely what makes threshold sessions unpredictable if you set intensity slightly too high—you can feel "okay," but metabolically and muscularly you are accumulating a bill that comes due 24-72 hours later.
There are exceptions. In some sessions, you will see an initially steep curve that quickly normalizes and flattens. Compare this against heart rate to check for deviation or balance. As mentioned earlier, quick heart rate rise, high pace, and low lactate is the ideal.
My experience is that in such sessions, muscle tone and elasticity are almost always close to optimal. The body is then highly receptive to training load. In a buildup period, this means you should clearly add extra running efforts to the session. In a peaking phase, you may choose to maintain the same session volume anyway, simply to bank that surplus.
An obvious risk of adding more training to sessions where the body is highly receptive is that pace, load, and session length naturally become tougher.
At such full green-light sessions, it is therefore important to take the easy day afterward seriously, using every available tool to normalize the muscles. If you come out of that day with extra soreness or elevated tone, do not be afraid to add an extra easy day.
This is something many miss. During peaking phases and highly receptive periods, it is important not to be afraid of extra rest days to consolidate the hard sessions. This can yield enormous performance gains. At signs of overload or peak readiness, pay extra attention to rest days.
Stabilization in the working range
The "good" threshold session is further characterized by finding a plateau after one to two efforts where lactate stabilizes near the desired level, and then maintaining that stability by adjusting pace minimally. This range will often be a zone of perhaps 0.3-0.6 mmol/L lactate, within which you move freely.
Drift through the session
Drift means lactate gradually rises even though pace remains the same. You hold the same tempo, but the curve creeps upward. Drift can be caused by heat, fluid loss, low fuel in the muscles, heavy surface, stiff muscles, or pauses that are too short. We must never forget that lactate is an indirect measure of load--though by a wide margin the best one readily available. Moderate drift can be acceptable. Steep drift at the same pace is a red flag—you are either too high, or the body is not receptive that day.
In sum, you train not just by numbers, but by curve shape.

An Operational Interpretation System:
The Five Session Types
These four elements-baseline, slope, stabilization, and drift-combine to produce recognizable patterns. Over years of profiling, I have come to classity sessions into five distinet types, each with its own implications for how you should respond.
The principle is simple: in practice, we measure lactate in the blood, not inside the working muscle. What we see is the net result of two simultaneous processes: lactate appearance and lactate removal. Lactate is formed primarily in working muscle when glycolytic flux is high and pyruvate is reduced to lactate to sustain energy production, and it is removed through uptake and oxidation in the heart and oxidative muscle (including oxidative fibers within the working muscle), as well as conversion to glucose in the liver.
Lactate is transported out of more glycolytic fibers largely via MCT4 and taken up by oxidative tissues largely via MCTI. These transport pathways are trainable, and well-trained athletes typically have a higher capacity to both export and import lactate than untrained individuals.
The curve therefore tells as much about transport and balance as about how hard the session is. The goal then becomes choosing intensity that delivers a high training effect at the lowest possible biological cost.
For classification to have value, some standardization is needed. You do not need a laboratory, but you need a consistent method. Choose a target range rather than a single value. Use a window you want to stay within during efforts.
Take samples at fixed time points after maintaining a steady pace. You want to see trends, not noise. Look at change over time at the same load.

Decision Rules in Practice
Knowing the five session types is one thing; knowing what to do with them in the moment is another. Here are the decision rules I have found most usefu
over the years:
1. Stabilize before you build volume
On long threshold efforts (for example, 6 × 2000 m) measure at least the fist two to three efforts to ensure you are in the right range. Once the value stabi-lizes, you can either "lock" the session or continue measuring.
Continuing to monitor is best, but if cost is a concern, choose to measure at the very start. Supplement ideally with measurements toward the end. The advantage of continuing to measure throughout the session is all the information it provides about current state, especially regarding session extension.
With repeated "green signals," I recommend adding extra running efforts, for example, one to two intervals at the very end.
2. Adjust pace cautiously
During lactate-guided sessions, it is rarely about dropping ten seconds per kilometer (16 seconds per mile). It is often about two to five seconds per kilometer (3-8 seconds per mile), or small adjustments in rest intervals and rhythm. If you must make large adjustments to hit the right lactate, either your form that day or standardization is off, and then it is often better to modify the session rather than force it into a template.
3. A clearly rising curve at the same pace is a stop signal with exceptions
If lactate rises repetition after repetition at the same pace and same pause, you have in practice already left the threshold range. You can "complete" by pushing, but then you have turned the session into something else, with a different cost.
For a model that must tolerate two threshold days per week and often double threshold, this is a poor trade.
There are, however, some exceptions. If you have completed a slightly too demanding session just before, or a hard race, this can show up in the curve,
precisely because tone is elevated.

In those cases, I have found it useful to continue the session to lower tone further, while still accumulating sufficient volume. I would then recommend lowering lactate from 2.3-3.0 mmol/L down to just above 2.0 mmol/L. This is then concluded with Smart Strides-smooth running efforts of 80-100 meters just above the threshold to break things up. You are then choosing to change intention within the threshold session itself.
I consciously used this principle after races, sometimes doing this directly after races with threshold efforts set somewhat lower, or the day after. You then accumulate threshold load, but with a slightly different intention-to lower muscle tone while still incorporating some elements of threshold training during a period when it must be balanced against more intensive training.
4. Use heart rate as a secondary signal
A high threshold heart rate combined with controlled lactate can indicate that the system is "open" and that the aerobic engine can work hard without tipping over.
For coaches, this means that if you use heart rate naively as a ceiling, you may at times limit athletes who are actually running well. Heart rate must be interpreted together with lactate curve, pace, and muscular response.
An amusing digression here: the renowned physiologist Stephen Seiler is mentioned in the training chapter regarding his contribution on 80/20 training. He lives only 1.7 km (about a mile) from me in the small city of Kristiansand—I can almost see his house. Several years ago, I had a conversation with him about precisely my observations on heart rate and lactate. He confirmed the theoretical basis for this and suspected, as I had observed, that braking mechanisms were likely involved.
We are back to the body's protective system.
Is it safe to open all the gates here?
In principle, though, this requires two things. First, that you do it with muscles that are actually functioning well. Second, with a body that has enough general surplus to allow opening up in that way. The duality is important to understand, and especially important in a peaking phase.
5. Use perception as a tertiary signal
Subjective perception, whether RPE or the extended talk test as described in Chapter 2, should be used actively throughout. This is the simplest signal to add, and it captures imbalances in the system, given that no measurements or models are completely accurate. Additionally, you should keep using the stair test and traffic light model, to provide a complete picture of receptivity.
Variation within the Lactate Range
The decision rules above assume you are aiming for a stable target, but there is also room for deliberate variation within the Golden Zone itself.
In the first article I wrote in 2021 about the Norwegian Method, I described parts of an intense experimentation phase within the Golden Zone:
*   Progressive sessions where lactate progressively increases from around 2.0 to 3.0 mmol/L over the course of the session, interval by interval.

*   Sessions where I would hold just below and up to 3.0 mmol/L and push this level as long and hard as possible.
*   "Floating" sessions where I would sit 0.4-0.8 mmol/L below the threshold.

Adjusting Long Intervals
Even with careful planning, sessions sometimes go off track. If during long intervals you get several efforts with lactate that is too high, you realistically have three choices: end the session, markedly reduce the load and restart the curve, or switch to shorter intervals.
All alternatives are possible, but often the most beneficial is to either end the session or switch to shorter intervals. The choice depends on two things.
First, what did your traffic light model show before the session? Check resting heart rate, HRV, warm-up heart rate, and ideally the stair test. If you were borderline and start missing on the curve, I recommend ending the session.
Alternatively, you can run some 30/30 intervals (30 seconds on, 30 seconds off) to break things up muscularly before trying again.
Second, if the parameters looked fine, it depends on where you are in the season. If you are approaching a tougher training period or the competition season, I recommend switching to shorter intervals. This can correct muscular imbalances that are beginning to build up, while maintaining some aerobic volume. If you are in the middle of winter in a buildup phase, the alternative may instead be to restart the curve with a lower starting pace.

These are very interesting questions for anyone training athletes at a high level. I appreciate both of these thought processes, and as mentioned earlier, an ideal system for elite athletes should probably contain elements of both aspects noted above. The challenge is, again, implementation in a safe manner and weighed against the core principles of the model.
I advocate simplification almost down to a primitive focus on what probably yields the greatest gains, before moving outward from there into experimental phases.
Choice of experimental elements should be athlete-specific and intention-spe-cific. We can, however, use lactate actively to accomplish this as safely as possi-ble. If an on/off model is used, lactate should be measured during the session.
This is challenging and must be done with assistance, and always at the same point in the active pauses.
The opposing systems question ties directly to the thinking about the two horses from Chapter 6 and drip load from the same chapter. This is also partly sport-specific. Running demands extreme muscular caution, and it is the only form of movement we carry from early childhood, with the impact loading that implies. We have narrower margins to work with here compared to many other sports.
As a Norwegian, I am very familiar with the training of cross-country skiers and the necessity of more dynamic work within sessions, because the terrain demands variation, especially in hills. One element is that the upper body is also used, but at the same time, if we applied the same intensity variation to a pure running session, the recovery time would be far longer.
We must always keep in mind the specific demands that running presents.
The Long-Term Thinking on More Intensive Training
These advanced considerations lead naturally to the question of how intensive training fits into the broader picture.
At the foundation lies a threshold-based focus. On top of this, there will always be a fixed element of more intensive training, but the frequency can vary. For some recreational runners, this can actually be done with weeks between sessions, with only focus on easy running and threshold training; for well-trained athletes, once a week as a template of sorts.
The fixed intensive element is thus fully open to individual planning.
Beyond this, elements like speed training and strength training, as well as potentially more than one intensive session per week (such as two sessions over a ten-day period), will be individually determined and phase-dependent. More explosive athletes will often tolerate this better; likewise, gradual adaptation over time builds tolerance far better than abrupt integration.
The reason I outlined such a simple transition from base training to competition season in earlier chapters, with short intervals that gradually become Longer at a lactate of 7-10 mmol/L, is because it provides a safe model that works for most people. Most people will make mistakes in this transition phase, and that is why I am conservative in my advice. That is also why this may appear
"too simple" compared to more complex models like those described above.
But if you constantly weigh training against your threshold value, factor in your muscular state, and understand how high your threshold pace must be for necessary performance, you can and should systematically think through the composition of more intensive sessions. For some, this will entail far greater amounts of intensive work in a session. For others, somewhat increased fre-quency. For others still, increased complexity.

Changing these variables requires monitoring the following closely:
*   The lactate curve within the intensive session—which systems does it trigger?
*   Adaptation to the given session —how the body responds when you repeat it over weeks, and how it affects threshold sessions in the same period.
If you run on/off training and see dramatically better lactate values within the session at a given pace week after week, while the curve is flat (meaning the aerobic pathway) and the threshold value remains stable in sessions before and after these more intensive sessions, this type of session gives you adaptations that are beneficial, underdeveloped, and may be worth focusing on further.
Again, you always stand at the fixed center and move outward with curiosity, but always with load, control, evaluation, and adjustment as guiding princi-ples. Experimentation with the model should be timed and phase-dependent.
I personally chose to use the fall each year for three to four months of extreme experimentation, before gradually returning to known elements.
Lactate Values during Experimentation
When experimenting with more intensive work, you also need guidelines for acceptable lactate ranges. Given a threshold value of around 3.0 mmol/L, my experience is that you should experiment in the 5-7 (8) mmol/L zone first.
There is enough stimulus here for real effect, while it is far safer than higher zones. As always, risk is weighed against reward
Practical Sample Collection
All of this depends, of course, on getting reliable lactate measurements in the first place. Lactate measurement in the field is simple in theory but full of potential errors in practice. The greatest cause of measurement errors is not the meter but user error in sample collection. Here is what you need to know to get reliable values.
Where should you prick?
You have two choices: fingertip or earlobe. Both work, but they do not give identical values. Blood samples from the fingertip show consistently higher lactate values than samples taken from the earlobe at the same time. The difference can be significant, with an average deviation in some studies of 0.66

mmol/L, and up to 0.86 mmol/L in the 4-8 mmol/L range. But even in the threshold range, the difference is substantial.
For running and cycling, research recommends the earlobe. During training on an ergometer or treadmill, there were no significant differences between venous samples and capillary samples from the ear, while fingertip values were higher. The earlobe may be preferred because it is less affected by lactate release from the arms and easier to sample.
The problem with the earlobe is that it requires a helper. If you are testing yourself, you must use the finger. The important thing is that you choose one site and stick to it. Do not compare values from the finger one day with the ear the next. Personally, I ran with the lactate meter in my pocket during sessions and pricked my own finger carlobe samples were impossible to manage alone.
Contamination is often the main problem
Sweat has much higher lactate concentration than blood and can significantly alter the reading. A single drop of sweat that mixes into the blood sample can give a completely wrong value. Contamination appears to be the single largest cause of measurement error. The smaller the blood sample the meter requires, the more likely contamination from sweat or oil on the skin becomes.
The protocol that works
Dry the area thoroughly with a towel or paper towel first. Remove all visible sweat from finger or ear, and preferably from hand and arm as well, since sweat can run down. Then clean with an alcohol swab and let the area dry completely before pricking. Alcohol residue can also contaminate the sample. After prick-ing, wipe away the first drop of blood to avoid contamination. Wipe away the first drop with a clean swab and test on the second.
Cold fingers give poor samples
In cold conditions, peripheral blood flow to the fingers drops, which can make sampling slow and readings less reliable. Some runners also have chronically poor finger perfusion. If your ngers are cold even at room remperature, use the earlobe.
Correct drop size
The blood drop should be round and stand up from the skin, not flat and runny.
If the sample is thin and watery, do not use it. A watery drop may mean contamination with sweat, or that the athlete is overhydrated. The drop should be 2-3 mm in diameter. If you do not get enough blood after ten seconds, prick again next to the original site instead of squeezing hard. Squeezing presses out tissue fluid that dilutes the sample.
Summary in Practice

What does all of this add up to in daily training? You establish a working range for threshold training, not a single threshold pace. You establish a connection between pace, heart rate, and lactate on a standardized day. You use profiling regularly to detect shifts. The curve moves to the right, or becomes steeper at the same pace. What you want is a robust way to set threshold sessions that deliver high aerobic load but low risk of the session escalating. You want a system that tells you when to push and when to hold back, before the body forces you to.
But the tool is only as good as its use. A lactate meter in the hands of someone who does not understand curve shape, drift, and error sources can do as much harm as good. The number alone says little. It is the change over time, the relationship with heart rate and pace, and the pattern through the session that give you the information you need.
It takes time to become good at this. You will miss things. You will misin-terpret. You will have sessions where you see in hindsight that you should have adjusted earlier. Over time, you build experience-how your body responds under different conditions, which patterns warn of problems, and which signal that you can push more. When it clicks, you can train more without the same cost. That is the entire point.
And once you can control intensity this precisely, the next step is obvious:
two quality sessions in one day, both kept inside the Golden Zone.
That is double threshold.
